Binance has warned its European users that it will stop providing crypto services in the EU after failing to secure a MiCA license before the deadline

On June 24, the exchange withdrew its license application in Greece and announced plans to apply in another EU country. However, with MiCA rules fully taking effect on July 1, time has run out. 

In emails sent to users, Binance's European entity stated that it can no longer accept new clients and will cease providing crypto-asset services from July 1, 2026.

Users in Poland, Italy, Spain, and France have already received instructions on how to withdraw their funds. 

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao criticized the decision, saying it's "sad to see the European Union deprive its users of access to the best liquidity in the world."

For now, this looks like a major setback for Binance in Europe and another reminder that regulation is becoming one of the biggest challenges for global crypto exchanges.

Truce on Paper, Live Fire in the Gulf

The U.S.–Iran ceasefire is already behaving like what it really is: a cease‑if‑you‑can‑get‑away‑with‑it. Bahrain reports Iranian attack drones over its territory hours after U.S. jets hit Iranian missile and radar sites. 

An oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz takes a projectile for the second time in days; both capitals accuse the other of “violating” an agreement they’re still trying to spin as a victory.

Each side is running the same script. Washington says Iran “foolishly” broke the truce by targeting a container ship, so it hits coastal systems along Hormuz and on Qeshm Island to prove it won’t blink first. 

Tehran frames its drone launches and strikes as self‑defense against U.S. aggression and vows to protect its “sovereignty and national interests with all its strength.” 

The result isn’t all‑out war, but a pattern of calibrated shots: enough to signal strength, not enough to collapse the deal.

Meanwhile, the shipping lane that was supposedly “reopened” by the memorandum is once again a hazard zone. 

Every new attack on a vessel like the Kiku pushes insurers and captains to rethink transit, even as Trump boasts of “record flows” through the strait and oil prices whipsaw around each incident. 

Energy markets briefly spike on news of attacks, then slip back toward pre‑war levels as traders bet that both Washington and Tehran still need the truce more than they need another escalation.

On the northern front, the U.S. tries to declare another win: an Israel–Lebanon arrangement under American sponsorship that asks the IDF to pull back from a sliver of southern Lebanese territory so the Lebanese army can step in, and quietly expects Hezbollah to fade into the background. 

Hezbollah’s leadership calls the deal “null and void” and promises to keep fighting, underlining again how often U.S. diplomacy in this war relies on getting armed actors to accept disarmament they never actually agreed to.

The war itself exposed the limits of U.S. power, the ceasefire formalized those limits, and now the “post‑war” phase is a controlled stress test. Neither side wants to go back to full‑scale bombardment; both are probing how far they can push without snapping the framework. 

On paper it’s de‑escalation; in practice it’s a live‑fire negotiation conducted by drones, tankers and carefully worded communiqués.

The Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish reverses its own aging process entirely. When damaged or old, it reverts back to its juvenile polyp stage and begins life again. It has been doing this for 500 million years. It cannot die of old age. It is literally immortal.

The naked mole rat lives 10 times longer than any rodent its size. It shows zero increase in mortality rate as it ages. Its cancer rate is effectively zero. Its cells do not deteriorate.

Greenland sharks live over 500 years. Bowhead whales over 200. Giant tortoises over 190.

Nature solved aging millions of years ago. In dozens of species. Through dozens of different mechanisms. The genetic code for indefinite cellular regeneration exists throughout the animal kingdom.

And it exists in you.

Human DNA contains the telomerase gene. It is active in your stem cells and reproductive cells right now—keeping them young indefinitely. The rest of your body ages because that gene is selectively silenced in somatic cells.

Not missing. Silenced.

The question is not “can humans stop aging?” The question is “why was the off-switch installed, and who benefits from keeping it on?”
